items.subtitle: What is Node2D?
items.contents:
What is Node2D?

Node2D is a 2D game engine and editor for creating games for the web. A project is built from Scenes, Nodes, Components, ScriptNodes, assets, input, physics, and runtime systems. A finished project can also be exported as a standalone web package and can optionally be configured as a Progressive Web App (PWA) for installable and offline-capable web use.

The editor is designed around a Node-based 2D world. You build the game visually, attach Components to Nodes, and use ScriptNodes to control behavior without writing the whole game as one large script.

  • Scenes hold the objects and camera used for a particular game screen or level.
  • Nodes are the objects in a Scene. Components give a Node its transform, visuals, physics, text, collisions, progress bars, and behavior.
  • ScriptNodes form the visual scripting graph owned by a Node's Script component.
  • Assets provide sprites, audio, and MIDI data used by Components and ScriptNodes.
  • The runtime executes the project during Play or Debug and maintains runtime copies of variables and object state.
  • The exporter can package the project as a web application and can generate a PWA manifest and service worker.

items.subtitle: How UIX fits together
items.contents:
How UIX fits together

A simple mental model is: Project → Scenes → Nodes → Components + ScriptNode graph → Runtime. Assets are project resources referenced by the Nodes and scripts. Input, camera, physics, audio, and UI systems operate around the Scene while the runtime is playing.

PartPurpose
ProjectContains Scenes, global variables, assets, game settings, and editor data.
SceneA collection of Nodes and folders plus a Scene Camera.
NodeAn individual game object or object container in a Scene.
ComponentA specific capability attached to a Node.
ScriptNodeA visual-logic block inside the Script graph owned by a Node.
AssetA reusable sprite, audio file, or MIDI resource.
RuntimeThe executing version of the project used by Play and Debug.

items.subtitle: Editor workflow
items.contents:
Editor workflow

  1. Create or load a project.
  2. Create Scenes and choose a Preferred Scene for Play/Debug.
  3. Create Nodes and arrange them in the Scene tree.
  4. Add or edit Components on Nodes.
  5. Open the Node's Script editor and build a ScriptNode graph.
  6. Create or import assets and select them from Sprite, Animation, and audio controls.
  7. Use the Scene Camera and Game Settings to define how the world is viewed.
  8. Play or Debug to test runtime behavior.
  9. Save the project locally or export an NDC/project package.

items.subtitle: Nodes
items.contents:
Nodes

A Node is the main object in a Scene. It has a name and numeric ID and owns Components such as Transform, Text, Sprite, Physics, Collider, Progress Bar, and Script.

The Node itself is not the same thing as a Component. The Node is the object; Components describe what the object looks like, how it moves, what it collides with, or what logic it executes.

Every Node has its own Script component and Transform component. The Node, Script, and Transform components are required by the editor and are not removable.

items.subtitle: Node IDs and names
items.contents:
Node IDs and names

A Node has a user-visible name and a positive whole-number numeric ID. Script selectors and object selectors can show nodes using a combined label such as Player [1]. Numeric IDs are used to identify runtime objects and to resolve object references.

Node names are not globally required to be unique in the same way numeric IDs are. Numeric IDs are normalized when Nodes are copied or imported so object references remain usable.

items.subtitle: Scene tree and folders
items.contents:
Scene tree and folders

The Scene tree can contain Nodes and folders. Folders are organization containers and can contain child Nodes or other folders.

  • Nodes can be moved into a folder or back to the Scene root.
  • Folders can be collapsed to reduce visual clutter.
  • Copy, paste, duplicate, delete, rename, and selection operations work from the tree and editor controls.
  • Deleting a folder deletes its contents after confirmation.

items.subtitle: ScriptNodes
items.contents:
ScriptNodes

Each Node has its own ScriptNode graph. The Script component opens the Script editor for that Node. ScriptNode positions, connections, and expressions are stored with that Node's graph.

Local variables belong to the same Node scope as its graph. A local variable named speed on one Node does not conflict with a local variable named speed on another Node.

items.subtitle: Script editor
items.contents:
Script editor

The Script editor is organized around three areas: the Local Variables panel, the ScriptNode Library, and the graph/inspector area. ScriptNodes are grouped into Events, Actions, and Controls.

  • Add a ScriptNode by clicking it in the library or by dragging it into the graph.
  • Select nodes to inspect and edit their input values.
  • Connect an output port to another ScriptNode input to route execution or data through the graph.
  • Use pan and zoom to navigate larger graphs.
  • Shift/Ctrl selection can be used for multiple ScriptNodes; copy, cut, paste, duplicate, delete, disconnect, and alignment/snap operations are available in the editor.

items.subtitle: Expressions
items.contents:
Expressions

A ScriptNode input can contain a normal value or an expression. Open the expression editor from an input to type or choose an expression.

String inputs are handled specially: when the expression editor is opened, a string that is not already a valid expression can be represented as a backtick literal so the literal text is preserved.

Expressions are evaluated with the current runtime context, so values such as ctx.global.score, ctx.local.speed, ctx.events.key.A, or Math.randInt(1,10) can be used where an input accepts an expression.

items.subtitle: Selection, view, and editing
items.contents:
Selection, view, and editing

The editor provides selection, move, rotate, scale, pan, zoom, centering, snapping, and context-menu operations. The workspace uses a Node-based scene view while separate panels handle components, scripts, assets, camera, game settings, and help.

Undo/redo uses editor snapshots. The current build keeps a finite history rather than an unlimited one.

items.subtitle: Copy and paste
items.contents:
Copy and paste

Node copy/paste duplicates a Node together with its Components and ScriptNode graph. ScriptNode IDs are remapped during duplication so pasted graphs do not accidentally reuse the source graph's internal identifiers.

Component copy/paste works from component context menus and replaces a same-type component when the destination already has one, where the component system allows replacement.

title: Components
items:
The Node component represents the object identity. It provides the Node name and numeric ID used by the editor and runtime.

  • Name: the object name shown in the Scene tree and selectors.
  • ID: a positive whole-number identifier used to reference the object.
  • Non-removable: every Node keeps this component.

The Script component owns the Node's visual ScriptNode graph. It is required on every Node and opens the Script editor.

  • Script name: the label shown for the component.
  • Graph: ScriptNodes and their connections are stored per Node.
  • Non-removable: every Node keeps its Script component.

Transform controls the Node's world position, scale, and angle.

PropertyMeaning
Position X/YWorld position of the Node.
Scale X/YHorizontal and vertical scale.
AngleNode rotation angle.
DefaultsPosition [0,0], Scale [1,1], Angle [0].

Transform is required and is used by drawing, physics, collisions, camera following, and runtime object movement.

The Text component draws text for the Node.

PropertyMeaning
TextString displayed by the Node.
Font SizeFont size in pixels; the editor enforces a positive minimum.
Font FamilyCSS font-family string such as sans-serif.
FG ColorText color.
BG ColorBackground/fill color behind the text.
BorderWhether text border rendering is enabled.
Border Color / WidthBorder appearance.
Corner RadiiTop-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left radius values.
PositionText offset/position values used by the component.

Text is optional and can be added or removed from a Node.

The Sprite component displays a Sprite asset or can reference an Animation from an Animation Sprite component.

  • Type: Sprite or Animation.
  • Sprite: selects a sprite asset when Type is Sprite.
  • Animation: selects an animation when Type is Animation.
  • Pixelated: controls pixel-art style sampling/rendering.

Animation Sprite stores one or more named animations. Each animation contains a sequence of sprite frames and an FPS value.

  • Animation name: identifier shown in the animation list.
  • FPS: playback frames per second, with a minimum of 1 in the editor.
  • Frames: sprite assets used by the animation.
  • Active Animation: the animation selected for playback/use.
  • The editor keeps at least one animation entry.

Physics makes a Node participate in the runtime physics system.

PropertyMeaning
BodyStatic, Kinematic, or Dynamic.
GravityGravity acceleration applied to Dynamic bodies.
FrictionSurface friction coefficient.
BouncinessRestitution value, constrained to the supported 0–1 range.
Fixed RotationPrevents rotational integration when enabled.
isColliderMarks the physics shape as a physical collision body.

The current runtime integrates Dynamic and Kinematic bodies. Dynamic bodies receive gravity. Collision solving can apply normal impulses, friction, restitution, and positional penetration correction.

Collider defines an explicit collision/detection shape and its local transform.

PropertyMeaning
ColliderEnable/disable the component for collision detection.
TypeRect, Circle, or Triangle.
Position X/YCollider local offset.
Scale X/YCollider local scale.
AngleCollider local rotation.
CollidableThe collider participates in collision detection when enabled.

The runtime supports rectangle/polygon, circle, and triangle collision shapes. A Physics component can also mark a physical body through its isCollider setting.

Progress Bar draws a value between a minimum and maximum using a background and fill region.

PropertyMeaning
Width / HeightVisual size.
ValueCurrent value.
Min / MaxValue range.
Position X/YLocal/world placement values used by the component.
BG ColorBackground color.
Fill ColorFilled portion color.
TL/TR/BR/BLCorner radius values.
Outline Color / SizeOutline appearance.
DirectionFill direction: left or right.
Defaults200×24, value 50, min 0, max 100.

Progress Bars are optional and can be added or removed like other visual Components.

items.subtitle: Variables
items.contents:
Variables

A variable stores a value that a script can read or change. UIX supports three main scopes: Global, Scene, and Local.

Variables are useful for scores, health, counters, state flags, names, settings, switches, timers, and other values that need to be shared or retained during runtime.

ScopeBelongs toExpression
GlobalWhole projectctx.global.variableName
SceneCurrent Scenectx.sceneVariables.variableName
LocalOne Nodectx.local.variableName

items.subtitle: Global Variables
items.contents:
Global Variables

Global variables belong to the whole project and can be accessed from different Scenes during runtime.

The expression form is ctx.global.variableName. Global names must be unique among the global variables.

Example: a global variable named score can be read with ctx.global.score.

items.subtitle: Scene Variables
items.contents:
Scene Variables

Scene variables belong to the current Scene. Every Scene has its own Scene-variable collection.

The expression form is ctx.sceneVariables.variableName. Runtime contexts can also expose scene-related values through the scene context.

A variable named score can exist separately in different Scenes because the collections are scene-scoped.

items.subtitle: Local Variables
items.contents:
Local Variables

Local variables belong to one specific Node and are visible to that Node's ScriptNode graph.

The expression form is ctx.local.variableName. Two different Nodes may each have a local variable with the same name because their local scopes are separate.

The Script editor shows the Local Variables section for the Node whose Script graph is open.

items.subtitle: Variable types
items.contents:
Variable types

The variable manager supports String, Bool, and Int variable types. ScriptNode inputs and expression fields additionally use representations for strings, integers, booleans, colors, selectors, and empty/null values where needed.

TypeTypical valueExample
StringText"Player"
BoolTrue/falsetrue
IntWhole number100
ColorColor string in expression-capable fields"#FFFFFFFF"
SelectorOne option from a generated list"Dynamic"

items.subtitle: Variable name errors
items.contents:
Variable name errors

The editor validates variable names. An empty or conflicting name is rejected. When a disallowed conflict is detected, the name field flashes with a red outline and returns to the previous valid value so the project is not left with an invalid variable collection.

items.subtitle: setVariable
items.contents:
setVariable

setVariable is an Action ScriptNode that changes a Global, Local, or Scene variable at runtime.

Inputs are Type, Name, and Value. The Name selector is populated from the variables available for the chosen scope.

Type = Global | Local | Scene
Name = variable name
Value = new value

items.subtitle: Runtime variable context
items.contents:
Runtime variable context

When a project starts, the runtime builds its execution context from the project variables and the current Scene/Node state. ScriptNodes read and modify the runtime values through their contexts.

This separates live play state from editor data while a game is running. The exact persistence of a runtime change depends on how the project is saved; playing a game is not the same as editing the source project value.

items.subtitle: What is a Scene?
items.contents:
What is a Scene?

A Scene is a collection of Nodes and folders that represents a level, screen, menu, room, or other game state.

A project can contain multiple Scenes. Each Scene also has its own Scene Camera and Scene-variable collection.

items.subtitle: Creating and managing Scenes
items.contents:
Creating and managing Scenes

  • Create a Scene to make another level or screen.
  • Rename a Scene to keep the project organized.
  • Delete a Scene when it is no longer needed; the project keeps at least one usable Scene.
  • Switching Scenes changes the Scene tree and the Scene-specific variables/camera data being edited.
  • A Preferred Scene is selected for starting Play and Debug.

items.subtitle: Preferred Scene
items.contents:
Preferred Scene

Game Settings → Preferred Scene chooses the Scene loaded first when Play or Debug starts. The selector is populated from the current project's Scenes.

If a saved Preferred Scene is no longer valid, UIX falls back to the first available Scene.

items.subtitle: Scene Camera
items.contents:
Scene Camera

The Scene Camera controls what part of the world is visible during runtime. The current camera model includes Enabled, Follow, Horizontal and Vertical movement, Animation mode, Speed, Scale, Position, Angle, and Background Color.

The default camera is enabled, follows this, uses Smooth animation at speed 300, scale 1, horizontal/vertical offsets 0, position [0,0], angle 0, and background color #202020.

items.subtitle: Camera Follow
items.contents:
Camera Follow

Camera Follow selects which Node the camera tracks. This means the current Node context; a specific Node can also be selected.

Follow is useful for player cameras where the camera should track a moving object during runtime.

items.subtitle: Camera movement and animation
items.contents:
Camera movement and animation

Quick camera movement applies the target directly. Smooth movement interpolates toward the target using the configured speed. Position, angle, scale, and offsets affect the final world projection.

items.subtitle: Camera Scale
items.contents:
Camera Scale

Camera scale changes how much world space is visible relative to the logical camera. A larger scale behaves like a wider view; a smaller scale behaves like a closer view, subject to the renderer's projection rules.

items.subtitle: Screen input and camera
items.contents:
Screen input and camera

Screen-space input and UI are interpreted through the logical screen projection used by the active screen type. World-space camera movement changes what world content is visible, while screen-space controls such as a Joystick stay anchored to the screen UI layer.

items.subtitle: Windowboxing
items.contents:
Windowboxing

Windowboxing is the default screen mode. The logical camera view is 1280×720 and is fitted inside the physical screen while preserving the 16:9 camera shape. Extra space becomes black bars.

items.subtitle: Stretch
items.contents:
Stretch

Stretch displays the 1280×720 logical canvas across the entire physical screen. When the physical aspect ratio differs from 16:9, the world can appear visually stretched.

items.subtitle: Crop
items.contents:
Crop

Crop scales the 1280×720 logical canvas until the physical screen is fully covered. This avoids black bars but crops world content outside the resulting camera frame.

items.subtitle: Smart Camera
items.contents:
Smart Camera

Smart Camera adapts the camera to the physical screen aspect ratio. The world is not stretched; instead the logical camera view becomes wider or narrower so the visible area matches the screen shape.

items.subtitle: Screen projection and input
items.contents:
Screen projection and input

All screen modes still use the camera transform for world rendering. UI and screen-space input use the same logical screen projection so controls remain associated with the screen instead of drifting with world camera movement.

items.subtitle: What is an Event?
items.contents:
What is an Event?

An event is a runtime signal that something happened, such as the game loading, a tick occurring, a key being pressed, a pointer action occurring, or a joystick changing.

Event ScriptNodes are placed at the beginning of a visual logic flow. Their output can connect to Actions and Controls.

items.subtitle: onLoad
items.contents:
onLoad

onLoad emits once when the runtime Scene loads. Use it for startup initialization such as setting starting values, choosing a sprite, or starting an audio effect.

items.subtitle: onTick
items.contents:
onTick

onTick emits on each runtime tick. Use it for repeated logic that must run continuously, such as movement or checking a game state.

items.subtitle: Keyboard Events
items.contents:
Keyboard Events

Keyboard event values are boolean one-shot pulses. For example, ctx.events.key.A becomes true for the runtime frame in which A is pressed.

The event system also supports identifier-safe modifier combinations such as ctx.events.key.CtrlS.

items.subtitle: onKeybind
items.contents:
onKeybind

onKeybind listens for the configured keybind selected in its Keybind input. Keybind choices include common letters, numbers, Enter, Space, Escape, modifiers, navigation keys, and other editor-supported keyboard identifiers.

Because editor keybinds are configurable, a project can use the same event concept for custom shortcuts instead of hard-coding a keyboard event everywhere.

items.subtitle: Touch and Mouse
items.contents:
Touch and Mouse

onTouch and onMouse respond to pointer events using an Event selector with up, down, or move.

The expression library exposes coordinate values such as ctx.TouchUpX, ctx.TouchUpY, ctx.MouseMoveX, and corresponding Down/Move values.

items.subtitle: Screen Input
items.contents:
Screen Input

onScreenInput is an event source for screen-space pointer input. It uses the same up, down, and move event selection and is useful for controls positioned in the logical screen UI layer.

items.subtitle: Joystick Events
items.contents:
Joystick Events

onJoystick fires for the selected joystick variable. A Scene can contain multiple Joysticks, each identified by its Variable name.

Joystick values are exposed through the expression library as distance, angle, and X/Y normalized values.

items.subtitle: onUnload
items.contents:
onUnload

onUnload runs before leaving the current runtime Scene. It can be used to perform exit/cleanup actions.

items.subtitle: Event delivery
items.contents:
Event delivery

During runtime, pointer events can be associated with a Node under the pointer, while keyboard, screen, and joystick events are broadcast when there is no specific target. The runtime clears one-shot keyboard event pulses after the runtime step so a press is not treated as held forever.

items.subtitle: ScriptNode groups
items.contents:
ScriptNode groups

The ScriptNode Library has three groups: Events start logic from runtime signals, Actions change game state, and Controls route or schedule logic.

GroupPurpose
EventsStart a flow when runtime events occur.
ActionsPerform a change or side effect.
ControlsBranch, schedule, or inspect conditions.

items.subtitle: onLoad (Events)
items.contents:
onLoad (Events)

No inputs. Emits out once when the runtime Scene loads.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onTick (Events)
items.contents:
onTick (Events)

No inputs. Emits out on each runtime tick.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onKeybind (Events)
items.contents:
onKeybind (Events)

Input: Keybind. Selects a keyboard key/keybind. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onTouch (Events)
items.contents:
onTouch (Events)

Input: Event = up, down, or move. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onMouse (Events)
items.contents:
onMouse (Events)

Input: Event = up, down, or move. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onScreenInput (Events)
items.contents:
onScreenInput (Events)

Input: Event = up, down, or move. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onJoystick (Events)
items.contents:
onJoystick (Events)

Input: Variable chooses a Scene joystick variable. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: onUnload (Events)
items.contents:
onUnload (Events)

No inputs. Emits out before leaving the runtime/current Scene.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: loadScene (Actions)
items.contents:
loadScene (Actions)

Input: Scene. Requests a runtime Scene change. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setVariable (Actions)
items.contents:
setVariable (Actions)

Inputs: Type (Global/Local/Scene), Name, Value. Changes a runtime variable. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setTransform (Actions)
items.contents:
setTransform (Actions)

Inputs: PosX, PosY, ScaleX, ScaleY, Angle. Changes the current Node transform. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setNode (Actions)
items.contents:
setNode (Actions)

Inputs: Name, Id. Changes the current runtime Node identity values. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setText (Actions)
items.contents:
setText (Actions)

Inputs: Text, PosX, PosY, FontSize, FontFamily, FG Color, BG Color, Border, Border Color, Border Width. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setSprite (Actions)
items.contents:
setSprite (Actions)

Inputs: Type (Sprite/Animation), Sprite, Animation, Pixelated. Changes the current Node's visual source. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setPhysics (Actions)
items.contents:
setPhysics (Actions)

Inputs: Body, Gravity, Friction, Bounciness, Fixed Rotation, isCollider. Changes runtime physics settings. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setCollider (Actions)
items.contents:
setCollider (Actions)

Inputs: Collider, Type (Rect/Circle/Triangle), PosX, PosY, ScaleX, ScaleY, Angle. Changes runtime collision shape/settings. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setProgressBar (Actions)
items.contents:
setProgressBar (Actions)

Inputs: Width, Height, Value, Min, Max, PosX, PosY, BG Color, Fill Color, TL, TR, BR, BL, Outline Color, Outline Size, Direction. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Follow Object (Actions)
items.contents:
Follow Object (Actions)

Input: Target node selector. Makes the current runtime object follow the chosen object according to the runtime follow behavior. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Destroy Object (Actions)
items.contents:
Destroy Object (Actions)

No inputs. Destroys the current runtime Node/object. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Create Object (Actions)
items.contents:
Create Object (Actions)

Inputs: Object, PosX, PosY, VelocityX, VelocityY, AngularVelocity. Creates a runtime copy/object based on a selected Node. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setVelocity (Actions)
items.contents:
setVelocity (Actions)

Inputs: VelocityX, VelocityY, AngularVelocity. Sets runtime velocity. Angular velocity is entered in degrees/second by the editor and converted by the runtime where required. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: setCamera (Actions)
items.contents:
setCamera (Actions)

Inputs: Enabled, Follow, PosX, PosY, Angle, Horizontal, Vertical, Animation (Quick/Smooth), Speed, Scale, BG Color. Changes the runtime Scene Camera. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: playAudio (Actions)
items.contents:
playAudio (Actions)

Inputs: src, duration, loop, fadein, fadeout. Plays an Audio or MIDI asset. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: stopAudio (Actions)
items.contents:
stopAudio (Actions)

No inputs. Stops runtime audio. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: clearAudio (Actions)
items.contents:
clearAudio (Actions)

No inputs. Stops runtime audio and clears the active runtime audio list. Output: out.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Boolean (Controls)
items.contents:
Boolean (Controls)

Input: Value (boolean). Outputs next (always true to continue), truth (Value is true), and falsy (inverse).

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Interval (Controls)
items.contents:
Interval (Controls)

Input: Milliseconds. When triggered, schedules repeated output at the configured interval. Output: out. Default: 1000 ms.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Timeout (Controls)
items.contents:
Timeout (Controls)

Input: Milliseconds. When triggered, schedules a one-shot delayed output. Output: out. Default: 1000 ms.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: isCollidedWith (Controls)
items.contents:
isCollidedWith (Controls)

Input: Target. Outputs truth when the current Node is colliding with the selected target and falsy otherwise.

ScriptNode connections are local to the Node's Script graph. Use the output ports to connect this node to another ScriptNode input.

items.subtitle: Expression context
items.contents:
Expression context

Expressions run against a context object named ctx. The context exposes variables, event state, transforms, velocity, input values, assets, Nodes, Scenes, joystick values, and runtime helpers.

items.subtitle: Variables in expressions
items.contents:
Variables in expressions

Use ctx.local.NAME, ctx.sceneVariables.NAME, and ctx.global.NAME for Local, Scene, and Global variables respectively.

ctx.local.speed
ctx.sceneVariables.level
ctx.global.score

items.subtitle: Keyboard expressions
items.contents:
Keyboard expressions

Keyboard event pulses are exposed as booleans. Letters can be accessed as identifiers, while keys that are not valid JavaScript identifiers can use bracket notation.

ctx.events.key.A
ctx.events.key.CtrlS
ctx.events.key["1"]

items.subtitle: Touch, Mouse, and Screen Input expressions
items.contents:
Touch, Mouse, and Screen Input expressions

The expression library exposes Up, Down, and Move coordinates for Touch, Mouse, and Screen Input.

  • Touch: ctx.TouchUpX, ctx.TouchUpY, ctx.TouchDownX, ctx.TouchDownY, ctx.TouchMoveX, ctx.TouchMoveY.
  • Mouse: corresponding ctx.Mouse... values.
  • Screen Input: corresponding ctx.Screen... values.

items.subtitle: Joystick expressions
items.contents:
Joystick expressions

For a joystick variable base name such as joystick, the expression library provides ctx.joystick_distance, ctx.joystick_angle, ctx.joystick_value_x, and ctx.joystick_value_y. Additional joysticks use their own variable names.

items.subtitle: Transform and velocity expressions
items.contents:
Transform and velocity expressions

The expression library exposes the current Node transform and velocity, including Position X/Y, Scale X/Y, Angle, Velocity X/Y, and Angular Velocity.

ctx.position.x
ctx.position.y
ctx.scale.x
ctx.scale.y
ctx.angle
ctx.velocity.velocityX
ctx.velocity.velocityY
ctx.velocity.angularVelocity

items.subtitle: Text, sprite, animation, and progress expressions
items.contents:
Text, sprite, animation, and progress expressions

When the Node has the relevant Component, expression groups can expose component data such as text, font size, font family, sprite name/source, animations, and progress-bar values.

items.subtitle: Math helpers
items.contents:
Math helpers

UIX adds helpers to the JavaScript Math object for expressions.

HelperPurpose
Math.lerp(a,b,t)Linear interpolation.
Math.clamp(v,min,max)Restrict a value to a range.
Math.map(v,inMin,inMax,outMin,outMax)Map one numeric range to another.
Math.moveTowards(current,target,maxDelta)Move toward a target by at most maxDelta.
Math.smoothstep(a,b,t)Smooth interpolation curve with clamped t.
Math.wrap(v,min,max)Wrap a number into a range.
Math.degToRad(degrees)Degrees to radians.
Math.radToDeg(radians)Radians to degrees.
Math.distance(a,b)2D distance between array-like [x,y] values.
Math.randInt(min,max)Returns a random integer using inclusive min and max bounds after numeric normalization.
Math.random()JavaScript random number helper.
Math.PI / Math.ECommon mathematical constants.
Math.pow, min, max, abs, sign, floor, ceil, round, trunc, sqrt, cbrt, exp, log, log10Standard numeric helpers.
Math.sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2, hypotTrigonometry and distance helpers.

items.subtitle: Vectors
items.contents:
Vectors

Vector helpers support common 2D operations using array-like vector values.

HelperPurpose
vec2(x,y)Create a 2D vector value.
length(v)Vector magnitude.
dot(a,b)Dot product.
normalize(v)Normalized vector.

items.subtitle: Physics overview
items.contents:
Physics overview

The runtime includes a 2D physics step used for Dynamic and Kinematic bodies. It handles gravity/integration, collision detection, contact response, friction, restitution, rotation, and penetration correction.

items.subtitle: Body types
items.contents:
Body types

BodyRuntime behavior
StaticDoes not integrate as a moving dynamic body; used as a stationary object.
KinematicIntegrates movement from its velocity without Dynamic gravity behavior.
DynamicIntegrates velocity and receives gravity; participates in physical collision response.

items.subtitle: Collision shapes
items.contents:
Collision shapes

The runtime currently supports Rect, Circle, and Triangle shapes. Rectangle and triangle geometry are treated as polygons; circles use circle-specific distance/projection checks.

items.subtitle: isCollider vs Collider
items.contents:
isCollider vs Collider

The Physics component's isCollider flag marks the physics body as a physical collision body. The Collider component separately defines an explicit collision/detection shape and local transform.

This lets a project use physics-body collision behavior and explicit Collider settings as separate concepts.

items.subtitle: Friction and bounciness
items.contents:
Friction and bounciness

Friction controls tangential resistance in contacts. Bounciness controls restitution, or how much separating velocity is restored after impact. The editor constrains bounciness to the supported 0–1 range.

items.subtitle: Fixed rotation
items.contents:
Fixed rotation

Fixed Rotation prevents angular motion integration for that body. This is useful for platformer characters, boxes that should never tip, or objects where rotation is controlled manually.

items.subtitle: Collision detection flags
items.contents:
Collision detection flags

The runtime tracks collision information so logic such as isCollidedWith can query whether objects are colliding. Debug rendering can also visualize collider shapes in the runtime preview.

items.subtitle: Physics limitations to remember
items.contents:
Physics limitations to remember

The current engine is a compact built-in 2D system rather than a full rigid-body physics framework. Game behavior should be designed around the supported body types and shapes, and values should be tested with the project's actual scale and camera settings.

items.subtitle: What is a UI Joystick?
items.contents:
What is a UI Joystick?

A UI Joystick is a screen-space input component for touch controls. It draws a circular base and knob and exposes a named variable that the runtime updates from the user's pointer movement.

items.subtitle: Joystick properties
items.contents:
Joystick properties

PropertyMeaning
VariableName used by expressions and onJoystick.
BG ColorJoystick base color.
Knob ColorJoystick knob color.
SizeWidth and height; default 110×110.
Left / Top / Right / BottomScreen anchor offsets. Unused anchors can be null.

The default joystick uses variable joystick, background #333333CC, knob #FFFFFFFF, size 110×110, left 10, bottom 10.

items.subtitle: Multiple Joysticks
items.contents:
Multiple Joysticks

The editor can create more than one joystick. The first default variable is joystick; additional joysticks use names such as joystick2, joystick3, and so on unless changed.

Joystick variables should remain uniquely named within the Scene so the input context can identify the intended control.

items.subtitle: Joystick expressions
items.contents:
Joystick expressions

Each joystick exposes a normalized X/Y value, distance, and angle through expression names based on its variable.

ctx.joystick_distance
ctx.joystick_angle
ctx.joystick_value_x
ctx.joystick_value_y

items.subtitle: Using onJoystick
items.contents:
Using onJoystick

Add an onJoystick Event ScriptNode and select the joystick Variable. Connect it to the Action or Control logic that should run when joystick input changes.

items.subtitle: What is the Asset Manager?
items.contents:
What is the Asset Manager?

The Asset Manager is the project resource area for Sprite, Audio, and MIDI assets. It lets you import files, create editable resources where supported, select assets from ScriptNodes/Components, and open the matching editor.

items.subtitle: Asset categories
items.contents:
Asset categories

CategoryExamplesUsed by
SpritesPNG, JPEG, SVG and project sprite framesSprite and Animation Sprite Components, setSprite
AudioMP3, WAV, OGG, M4A and supported audio resourcesplayAudio
MIDIMID/MIDIMIDI Editor, playAudio

items.subtitle: Importing assets
items.contents:
Importing assets

The importer classifies files using their extension/MIME type. MIDI files are recognized as MIDI, audio MIME types and common audio extensions become Audio, and image/SVG input becomes Sprite.

Asset names are derived from filenames and are deduplicated when necessary, using suffixes such as 2 or 3.

items.subtitle: Sprite assets
items.contents:
Sprite assets

Sprite assets can be opened in the Sprite Editor for pixel editing. Imported raster or SVG images become usable sprite image data in the project.

items.subtitle: Audio assets
items.contents:
Audio assets

Audio assets are selectable by name in the playAudio ScriptNode. Runtime audio can support duration, looping, fade-in, and fade-out settings where the playback path supports them.

items.subtitle: MIDI assets
items.contents:
MIDI assets

MIDI assets use the bundled offline MIDI parser/encoder. They can be opened in the MIDI Editor, exported back to .mid, and played at runtime through the built-in Web Audio based MIDI playback path.

items.subtitle: Asset persistence
items.contents:
Asset persistence

The Asset Manager does not maintain a separate cloud asset library. Assets belong to the current project state and are included in project data so NDC import/export can restore them with the project.

items.subtitle: Deleting and editing
items.contents:
Deleting and editing

Assets can be selected, removed, or opened in the appropriate editor. Sprite and MIDI resources expose editing paths; ordinary audio is used as imported source data.

items.subtitle: Sprite Editor overview
items.contents:
Sprite Editor overview

The Sprite Editor is a pixel-oriented editor for creating and editing sprite assets and sprite animation frames. It works with rasterized image content and can manage multiple frames.

items.subtitle: Create a Sprite
items.contents:
Create a Sprite

New Sprite asks for a name and dimensions. Width and height are constrained to a practical 1–512 pixel range, and a new sprite starts with at least one frame.

items.subtitle: Drawing tools
items.contents:
Drawing tools

The editor provides tools for common pixel-art operations.

  • Pencil for freehand pixels.
  • Eraser for removing pixels.
  • Line for straight segments.
  • Point for single points.
  • Rectangle for rectangular shapes.
  • Circle/Ellipse for rounded shapes.
  • Triangle for triangular shapes.
  • Fill/bucket for connected-region fills.
  • Perfect Shape for geometry-constrained drawing where supported.

items.subtitle: Brush and color
items.contents:
Brush and color

Brush size can be adjusted, and a color picker controls the drawing color. The editor supports common pixel-editing operations without requiring an external graphics program.

items.subtitle: Mirror, flip, and rotate
items.contents:
Mirror, flip, and rotate

The editor provides Mirror X/Y for drawing symmetry and Flip X, Flip Y, and Rotate operations for transforming the image/selection.

items.subtitle: Selection tools
items.contents:
Selection tools

Box and lasso selection can isolate pixels for cut, copy, paste, and transformation. Modifier keys can add or subtract from a selection. Selected pixels can be moved using the selection gizmo.

items.subtitle: Frames and animation
items.contents:
Frames and animation

A sprite resource can contain multiple frames. The editor provides previous/play/next controls, frame ordering, frame deletion, and FPS control. Frames can be reordered in the animation editor.

items.subtitle: Sprite saving
items.contents:
Sprite saving

Saving a sprite writes its frames back into the project as image assets. Each animation frame can be represented as a separate PNG resource used by Animation Sprite.

items.subtitle: Grid and zoom
items.contents:
Grid and zoom

The editor supports grid display, centering, and large zoom ranges for pixel-level work. Pinch/zoom support is available in the mobile-oriented editing path.

items.subtitle: MIDI Editor overview
items.contents:
MIDI Editor overview

The MIDI Editor is an offline piano-roll style editor for composing and editing note sequences. It includes note drawing, erasing, moving, resizing, track management, BPM, snap/length controls, waveform preview, looping, MIDI import, and MIDI export.

items.subtitle: Tracks
items.contents:
Tracks

A MIDI file can contain multiple tracks. The editor provides a track panel with track names and colors and lets you add or delete tracks while keeping at least one track.

items.subtitle: Notes
items.contents:
Notes

A note has a time position, duration, pitch, and velocity. Pitch follows standard MIDI note numbering from 0–127. Notes can be created, moved, resized, copied, pasted, duplicated, or erased.

items.subtitle: Drawing and erasing
items.contents:
Drawing and erasing

Use Draw to place notes and Erase to remove notes. Snap settings determine the timing grid used for editing and new note positions.

items.subtitle: Snap and length
items.contents:
Snap and length

Snap options include values such as 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, and Bar. Length controls provide matching rhythmic note lengths for fast entry.

items.subtitle: BPM and playback
items.contents:
BPM and playback

BPM is editable in the supported range and controls musical playback timing. Play, Stop, Rewind, and Loop controls are available for preview.

items.subtitle: Waveform preview
items.contents:
Waveform preview

The preview synthesizer uses basic oscillator waveforms such as sine, triangle, square, and sawtooth. The waveform is a preview/playback characteristic, not MIDI file data itself.

items.subtitle: Multi-selection and clipboard
items.contents:
Multi-selection and clipboard

Shift/Ctrl selection, marquee selection, duplicate, copy, paste, and paste-at-cursor are supported. The selection is highlighted so groups of notes can be edited together.

items.subtitle: MIDI import
items.contents:
MIDI import

The bundled parser reads MIDI files without an external MIDI library. Imported note data preserves track names/channels and note pitch/duration/velocity information supported by the editor.

items.subtitle: MIDI export
items.contents:
MIDI export

Export writes the project MIDI data back to a standard .mid file using the bundled encoder.

items.subtitle: Runtime MIDI playback
items.contents:
Runtime MIDI playback

The runtime can play MIDI assets through playAudio. The bundled runtime playback path parses MIDI and uses Web Audio oscillator tones for audible preview/playback.

items.subtitle: Undo and editing
items.contents:
Undo and editing

The MIDI editor keeps an undo/redo history for note and track edits so composition changes can be reverted without rebuilding the file.

items.subtitle: Audio playback
items.contents:
Audio playback

The playAudio ScriptNode plays a selected Audio or MIDI asset. Inputs include duration, loop, fade-in, and fade-out.

items.subtitle: stopAudio
items.contents:
stopAudio

stopAudio stops active runtime audio playback.

items.subtitle: clearAudio
items.contents:
clearAudio

clearAudio stops runtime audio and clears the runtime audio list.

items.subtitle: Audio selectors
items.contents:
Audio selectors

Audio selectors are populated from project Audio and MIDI assets. The selected asset is referenced by name in the ScriptNode.

items.subtitle: New Project
items.contents:
New Project

A new project starts with a default project name, a Main Scene, standard game settings, and the required project structures. The initial screen type is Windowboxing.

items.subtitle: Local projects
items.contents:
Local projects

UIX can save project data into local browser storage/IndexedDB. The local project list supports loading and managing saved project records.

items.subtitle: Save in Project
items.contents:
Save in Project

File → Project → Save in Project stores the current project data as an NDC project record. Ctrl+S uses the same save concept.

items.subtitle: Export .ndc
items.contents:
Export .ndc

Exporting the project creates a Node Compressed Data (NDC) file containing project information and binary assets. It is intended as the portable project format for UIX.

items.subtitle: Import .ndc
items.contents:
Import .ndc

Import restores Scenes, ScriptNode graphs, variables, UI data, and binary assets from the project NDC data.

items.subtitle: NDC compression
items.contents:
NDC compression

The bundled ndcCodec.js contains the offline NDC codec. The project text is compressed using a compact dictionary/pair approach and additional passes stop when the next pass would not make the result smaller. The current NDC4 path stores binary assets without requiring Base64 in the NDC container and remains compatible with earlier NDC generations supported by the codec.

items.subtitle: Project safety
items.contents:
Project safety

Saving a project is different from Play/Debug. Play creates runtime state for execution; Save/Export writes the editor project state so it can be reopened later.

items.subtitle: Export Project
items.contents:
Export Project

The Project Exporter builds a standalone web package containing an index.html, the current project.ndc, and the runtime/editor engine files required for playback.

items.subtitle: Exported runtime files
items.contents:
Exported runtime files

The exporter packages the core runtime modules including node.js, assets.js, scriptNodes.js, uiComponents.js, ndcCodec.js, runtimeEngine.js, and app.js. The bundled midiParser.js is included when MIDI support is needed.

items.subtitle: PWA mode
items.contents:
PWA mode

The exporter can optionally generate a PWA configuration. When enabled, it writes a manifest.json and a service worker that caches the exported application files so the web app can be installed and used with offline caching behavior.

items.subtitle: PWA manifest
items.contents:
PWA manifest

The PWA editor supports App Name, Short Name, Start URL, Display mode, Orientation, Theme Color, Background Color, Description, and raw manifest JSON editing. The exporter fills standard values from the project when fields are not overridden.

items.subtitle: PWA icon
items.contents:
PWA icon

An optional icon asset can be selected for the exported manifest. Supported icon source handling includes SVG/PNG conversion paths used by the exporter.

items.subtitle: Screen type in export
items.contents:
Screen type in export

Standalone exports carry the chosen screen type so runtime playback uses the intended Windowboxing, Stretch, or other supported screen behavior.

items.subtitle: Play
items.contents:
Play

Play starts the project using the Preferred Scene and the configured game settings. Runtime input, scripts, camera, physics, audio, variables, and object changes are active during execution.

items.subtitle: Debug
items.contents:
Debug

Debug runs the same runtime systems while exposing development information such as debug variables and runtime state where enabled.

items.subtitle: Runtime Script execution
items.contents:
Runtime Script execution

Event nodes produce signals. Receiver/action nodes run when their input execution signal reaches them. Controls such as Boolean branch outputs, Interval, and Timeout can route or schedule further execution.

items.subtitle: Runtime object changes
items.contents:
Runtime object changes

Actions such as Create Object, Destroy Object, setTransform, setVelocity, setPhysics, setCollider, setText, setSprite, and setProgressBar operate on runtime object state. These changes are part of the running game state until execution ends or a new Scene is loaded.

items.subtitle: Scene changes at runtime
items.contents:
Scene changes at runtime

loadScene sets a pending Scene change. The runtime then switches to the selected Scene and reinitializes its runtime context for that Scene.

items.subtitle: Debug variables
items.contents:
Debug variables

Variables can be marked for debugging in the editor. Debug-enabled variable information can be surfaced by the runtime Debug UI to make game-state inspection easier.

items.subtitle: Keyboard shortcuts
items.contents:
Keyboard shortcuts

The Help page also loads the live keybind definitions from js/keyBinds.js. The main commands in this build include:

items.subtitle: MIDI shortcuts
items.contents:
MIDI shortcuts

MIDI editing uses the shared command system plus MIDI-specific commands such as Save MIDI, Export MIDI, Import MIDI, and Duplicate Selection.

items.subtitle: Sprite shortcuts
items.contents:
Sprite shortcuts

Sprite editing includes the shared command handling and a Save Sprite shortcut through the sprite editor.

items.subtitle: Custom keybinds
items.contents:
Custom keybinds

Editor keybinds are configurable in Editor Settings. Changes are stored locally and can be reset to defaults.

items.subtitle: Color values
items.contents:
Color values

Color editors support RGBA-style values and text forms including #RGB, #RRGGBB, #RRGGBBAA, and rgb()/rgba() input paths supported by the editor.

items.subtitle: Boolean inputs
items.contents:
Boolean inputs

Boolean ScriptNode inputs use true/false controls. The Boolean Control node exposes three outputs so one condition can explicitly route to truth, falsy, or a next/continue path.

items.subtitle: Integer inputs
items.contents:
Integer inputs

Integer inputs are used for whole-number values such as positions, sizes, milliseconds, BPM-related settings, and other fields where the editor defines integer input behavior.

items.subtitle: Selector inputs
items.contents:
Selector inputs

Selector inputs generate their choices from the current Scene, Nodes, variables, assets, animations, joystick list, or other available project data. This means the selector can change when the underlying project changes.

items.subtitle: Null and automatic values
items.contents:
Null and automatic values

Some ScriptNode inputs use null to mean that no override was entered. At runtime, the action can then preserve the existing value or use its component default/normalization path.

items.subtitle: Help system
items.contents:
Help system

The Help page loads help/help.json and builds a searchable navigation tree from its title, subtitle, and contents fields. Contents are rendered as HTML.

items.subtitle: Help JSON format
items.contents:
Help JSON format

[
  {
    "title": "Section Name",
    "items": [
      {
        "subtitle": "Topic",
        "contents": "
Topic
Explanation...
"
      }
    ]
  }
]

Use a JSON array at the root. Each section has title and items; each item has subtitle and contents. Since the current Help renderer uses innerHTML, write headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, and code blocks as HTML.

items.subtitle: Common variable error
items.contents:
Common variable error

A variable name conflict usually means the new name already exists in a scope where duplicate names are not allowed. The editor intentionally restores the previous valid name instead of leaving the invalid one in project state.

items.subtitle: Common ScriptNode issue
items.contents:
Common ScriptNode issue

When a ScriptNode does not appear to run, check that an Event node actually emits, that its output is connected to the intended receiver input, and that the current Node/Scene is active at runtime.

items.subtitle: Common asset issue
items.contents:
Common asset issue

When an asset cannot be selected, verify that it was imported into the current project and that the ScriptNode/Component selector is using the matching asset category.

items.subtitle: Common camera issue
items.contents:
Common camera issue

If the world appears stretched, cropped, or boxed unexpectedly, check Game Settings → Screen Type and then check the Scene Camera scale, position, follow, and offsets.

items.subtitle: Common MIDI issue
items.contents:
Common MIDI issue

If MIDI preview differs from a hardware/software synthesizer, remember that UIX runtime preview uses the bundled Web Audio oscillator path rather than reproducing an external instrument's exact sound bank.

items.subtitle: All Components
items.contents:
All Components

Node, Script, Transform, Text, Sprite, Animation Sprite, Physics, Collider, Progress Bar.

items.subtitle: All ScriptNodes
items.contents:
All ScriptNodes

onLoad, onTick, onKeybind, onTouch, onMouse, onScreenInput, onJoystick, onUnload, loadScene, setVariable, setTransform, setNode, setText, setSprite, setPhysics, setCollider, setProgressBar, Follow Object, Destroy Object, Create Object, setVelocity, setCamera, playAudio, stopAudio, clearAudio, Boolean, Interval, Timeout, isCollidedWith.
